1. Dystrophinopathies.

Duvuru R(1), Cunningham T(1), Colvin MK(2), Veerapandiyan A(1).

In: Adam MP, Bick S, Mirzaa GM, Wallace SE, Amemiya A, editors. GeneReviews(®) 
[Internet]. Seattle (WA): University of Washington, Seattle; 1993–2026.
2000 Sep 5 [updated 2026 Sep 10].

Author information:
(1)University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences;, Arkansas Children's Hospital, 
Little Rock, Arkansas
(2)Massachusetts General Hospital;, Harvard Medical School, Boston, 
Massachusetts

CLINICAL CHARACTERISTICS: The dystrophinopathies comprise a spectrum including 
Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) and Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD), which 
predominantly affect males and involve skeletal and cardiac muscle, and 
DMD-related cardiomyopathy, characterized by cardiac muscle involvement 
typically without symptomatic skeletal muscle involvement that affects both 
males and females. DMD is characterized by early onset and progressive weakness, 
motor delays, increased risk of cognitive issues, neurobehavioral and 
psychiatric manifestations, progressive respiratory issues, decline in cardiac 
function, constipation, osteopenia, and Increased mortality. BMD is 
characterized by later onset and slower progression, a more heterogeneous 
cardiac phenotype, and longer survival. Longevity in those with 
dystrophinopathies has increased with development of improved therapies.
DIAGNOSIS/TESTING: The diagnosis of a dystrophinopathy is established in a 
proband with suggestive clinical and laboratory findings and a hemizygous or 
heterozygous pathogenic variant in DMD identified by molecular genetic testing.
MANAGEMENT: Corticosteroid therapy: Prednisone, deflazacort, or vamarolone for 
improved muscle strength and motor function Targeted therapies: Histone 
deacetylase inhibitor therapy (givinostat); dystrophin restoration therapy 
(antisense oligonucleotide, adeno-associated virus-mediated gene therapy) for 
those with DMD pathogenic variants in select exons Supportive care: In affected 
males – preventative home stretching; orthotics; mobility and seating equipment; 
pain management; treatment of scoliosis per neuromuscular specialist and 
orthopedist; regular submaximal aerobic exercise or exercise as tolerated; 
progressive mobility planning; developmental and educational support; standard 
treatment of neurobehavioral and psychiatric manifestations; nutrition support; 
gastrostomy tube when needed; proactive treatment of gastroesophageal reflux and 
constipation; treatment of cardiac disease per cardiologist; vaccinations for 
respiratory illnesses; respiratory spirometry, lung volume recruitment, 
mechanical insufflation-exsufflation; additional respiratory support when 
needed; prompt treatment of respiratory infection; bisphosphonates, vitamin D, 
and calcium supplements to prevent fractures; transitional care plan; family and 
social work support. In heterozygous females – cardiac management per 
cardiologist; regular exercise as tolerated, stretching, and physical therapy as 
needed in those with skeletal muscle manifestations. Surveillance: In affected 
males – measure linear growth every six months until completion of puberty and 
attainment of adult height; nutrition assessment by a registered nutritionist at 
each visit and at least every six months; assessment of skeletal muscle 
involvement by a neuromuscular neurologist and physical therapist every six 
months; cardiology evaluation including EKG and echocardiogram or cardiac MRI 
annually and before major surgery and more frequently in those with myocardial 
fibrosis or ventricular dysfunction; Holter monitor annually in those with 
cardiac dysfunction; evaluation by speech and language therapist when dysphagia 
is suspected; evaluation for gastrointestinal manifestations per 
gastroenterologist; pulmonology assessment annually and every six months after 
loss of ambulation; assess for cognitive and educational issues at each visit; 
neuropsychological evaluation as needed; assess for anxiety, depression, and 
social concerns at every visit; psychiatry evaluation as needed; assess pubertal 
development at each visit beginning in early adolescence; endocrinology 
evaluation in those with absence of pubertal development by age 14 years; 
clinical spine examination at each visit; spine radiographs in those with 
evidence of scoliosis; assess for back pain and fractures at each visit in those 
on steroid therapy; consider annual lateral spine imaging and dual-energy x-ray 
absorptiometry scan. In heterozygous females – cardiac evaluation with EKG and 
cardiac imaging every three to five years beginning in the 2nd to 3rd decade of 
life; cardiac follow up per cardiologist in those with cardiac manifestations; 
assessment of skeletal manifestations every 2-3 years. Agents/circumstances to 
avoid: Abrupt discontinuation of corticosteroids; stress dosing is recommended 
for steroid therapy to avoid adrenal crisis; statins may exacerbate muscle 
weakness and cause rhabdomyolysis; anesthetics such as succinylcholine can 
trigger malignant hyperthermia. Evaluation of relatives at risk: Evaluate 
at-risk male relatives of an affected individual in order to identify as early 
as possible those who would benefit from prompt initiation of supportive care 
and dystrophin restoration targeted therapy. Evaluate at-risk female relatives 
to identify those who would benefit from cardiac and skeletal muscle evaluation 
and surveillance. Evaluations include molecular genetic testing if the DMD 
pathogenic variant in the family is known. Pregnancy management: Evaluation for 
dilated cardiomyopathy and skeletal muscle involvement ideally prior to 
conceiving or as soon as pregnancy is recognized; women with dilated 
cardiomyopathy should be managed by a cardiac specialist with experience in 
treatment of heart failure and/or neuromuscular disorders and a high-risk 
obstetrician.
GENETIC COUNSELING: Dystrophinopathies are inherited in an X-linked manner. Male 
proband: The risk to sibs depends on the genetic status of the mother. If the 
mother of the proband is heterozygous for a DMD pathogenic variant, the chance 
of the mother transmitting the pathogenic variant in each pregnancy is 50%. 
Males who inherit the DMD pathogenic variant will be affected and will typically 
have clinical manifestations similar to those of the proband. Females who 
inherit the pathogenic variant will be heterozygotes and at risk for DMD-related 
cardiomyopathy. Heterozygous females are mostly free of severe skeletal muscle 
disease but may have milder muscle involvement or, rarely, a DMD or BMD 
phenotype resulting from non-random X-chromosome inactivation. Female proband: 
The risk to sibs depends on the genetic status of the parents. If the mother of 
the proband has a DMD pathogenic variant, the chance of the mother transmitting 
it in each pregnancy is 50%. If the father of the proband has a DMD pathogenic 
variant, he will transmit it to all his daughters and none of his sons. Once the 
DMD pathogenic variant has been identified in an affected family member, 
identification of female heterozygotes and prenatal testing are possible. 
Depending on the familial DMD pathogenic variant, preimplantation genetic 
testing may be an option for some families but can be challenging if phasing is 
necessary to confirm test results.
